claim: The long (higher-CAPM-alpha) legs of the value, profitability, investment, low-risk, and payout equity risk factors all share the common economic feature of investing in firms with SHORT cash-flow duration -- specifically firms with high book-to-market, high operating profitability, low asset growth, low market beta, and HIGH payout ratio.
stance_target: the analytical point that a mega-cap with a high payout ratio (like Apple) should be classified as relatively short-duration, not long-duration, within this asset-pricing framework
scope_conditions: US and global equities, 1929-2019 (dividend/growth data) and 1990-2019 (broad sample)
quoted_support: We find that the risk factors invest in firms that have a short cash-flow duration... firms with low investment and high payout ratios... invest only sparsely in future projects, [so] they also imply that these firms will have low growth and thus a short cash-flow duration.

claim: Using single-stock dividend futures (dividend strips) from 2010-2019, the CAPM alpha on an individual firm's cash-flow claim decreases smoothly with the claim's maturity -- from approximately 8% per year for a 1-year claim to approximately 4% per year for a 4-year claim -- and this maturity-alpha relationship is nearly identical for value and growth firms alike.
stance_target: the duration/rate-sensitivity premium attaches to the maturity of a specific cash-flow claim, not to a firm's growth/value label -- meaning firms that return cash sooner (via buybacks) hold a genuinely different risk profile than their headline growth narrative might suggest
quoted_support: the alphas start at around 8% per year for the one-year claim and decrease to around 4% for the four-year claim. Moreover, for each maturity, the risk-adjusted returns are almost the same for both legs of the risk factors... for instance, the three-year claim on a value firm has the same risk-adjusted return as the three-year claim on a growth firm.

claim: High-profit firms have short cash-flow duration because they have large profits today relative to the present value of future profits, paralleling the logic that high-payout, low-investment firms also have short duration.
stance_target: profitability and payout are both markers of short effective duration
scope_conditions: general firm cash-flow accounting logic underlying the factor construction
quoted_support: high-profit firms have short duration because they have large profits today relative to the value of future profits.
